hindi: माना कि $f:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ एक अवकलनीय फलन है जिसके लिए सभी $x>0$ हेतु $xf'(x)-f(x)=x^{2}\left(1+\ln x\right)$ तथा $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0^{+}}\dfrac{f(x)}{x}=1$ है। तब $f(e)$ बराबर है
solution: Linear form $f'-\dfrac{1}{x}f=x(1+\ln x)$ has IF $\dfrac1x$; by inspection $\dfrac{xf'-f}{x^{2}}=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{f}{x}\right)$
$x\ln x\to0$ as $x\to0^{+}$, so the limit condition gives $C=1$
solution_full: Write the equation as $f'(x)-\dfrac{1}{x}f(x)=x(1+\ln x)$, a linear equation with $P=-\dfrac1x$. The integrating factor is $e^{-\int dx/x}=\dfrac1x$ on $(0,\infty)$.

Multiplying by the integrating factor is the same as dividing the original equation by $x^{2}$, and the left side is then an exact derivative: $\dfrac{xf'(x)-f(x)}{x^{2}}=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{f(x)}{x}\right)$.
The right side becomes $1+\ln x$. Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)=\ln x+1$, it is also an exact derivative.
Now $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0^{+}}x\ln x=0$, so $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0^{+}}\dfrac{f(x)}{x}=C$. The given limit is $1$, so $C=1$.
Option (C) results from integrating $1+\ln x$ as $x+x\ln x$ (forgetting that $\int\ln x\,dx=x\ln x-x$); option (A) from taking $C=0$.
originality_note: New: a linear equation whose constant is fixed not by a value of f but by the limit of f(x)/x at the singular end x = 0, where x ln x vanishes (way 5). Closest known: xy' - y = x^2 type textbook equations with y(1) given. Different because: the condition at x -> 0+ needs the limit of x ln x and decides the constant.
